parts.text:
You are working for a client on a new software service. Nobody has designed it yet.

The client writes:

> Our customer companies need a new service for running their drone fleets from day to day, on our platform. Write the requirements for it: what the service must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does.

What you know about the client's business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The people who will use the service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You can reach one person in each role. A message that is exactly one line, `ASK <role>: <question>`, with `<role>` one of `technician`, `dispatcher` or `desk`, goes to that person, and their answer comes back to you. Each of them remembers what you asked them before. You can send at most 90 such questions in all. Any other message is taken as your requirements, and ends the work.

Write the requirements as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, with nothing else in that message:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
ASK technician: What are your day-to-day responsibilities, and what do you need the service to do for you regarding drones, batteries, equipment, and maintenance?

As a fleet technician, my job is to keep our drones and charging equipment in working order. I add new drones to the fleet, retire old ones, set up our charging pads at our sites, take drones out of service for repairs and put them back, and send drones to charge. Regulators can also ask us to show how our drones have been looked after.
ASK dispatcher: What are your day-to-day responsibilities, and what do you need the service to do for you regarding jobs, routes, drones, and sites?

I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I plan and run them by deciding which drone flies and along which way, and signing off a flight before it leaves. I can call off a flight. Choosing the drone and the way it flies is my legal responsibility, and our company's policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us, though we do want help finding out which of our drones could get to where a job starts. Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time.
ASK desk: What are your day-to-day responsibilities, and what do you need the service to do for you regarding airspace, authorities, and drone operators?

I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which includes the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers. I work for all customer companies and have no business looking into any one company's operations.
ASK technician: What information needs to be recorded when adding a new drone, retiring a drone, or taking a drone out of service for repair and putting it back?
ASK technician: What specific actions do you take with drones and charging pads, and what rules or constraints apply to them?

I add new drones to the fleet, retire old ones, set up our charging pads at our sites, take drones out of service for repairs and put them back, and send drones to charge. Our company runs a few hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers, which differ in payload capacity, range, sensors, and charging connectors. We have a few dozen charging pads at our own sites, and pads are never lent to another company.
ASK technician: How does charging work, what are the rules for sending a drone to a charging pad, and how do charging connectors or sites affect it?

I send drones to charge, and we have a few dozen charging pads at our own sites that are never lent to another company. Several connector types are in use, and they are not interchangeable. Batteries also drain faster in cold and wind than planned.
